name: topmodel
assumed_learner_prerequisites: Professional software development using Python, C, or C++
Secondary-school algebra and arithmetic; no assumed hydrology, calculus, or numerical-modeling education
required_topics: What the scientific model claims: Distinguish a calculated result from a measurement of the catchment; State what question the model answers and what quantities it does not predict; Describe the real-world story that the equations simplify; Express that story with quantities, rules and assumptions; Distinguish an equation from the time-stepping procedure used to calculate it; Explain why a physically motivated formula can still simplify or misrepresent a real place; Separate changing weather, chosen settings, remembered water, results and checking quantities; Distinguish how a run starts from what enters or leaves while it runs; Recognize that one model may contain all three; Connect a scientific claim to a paper section or exact code revision; do not let a familiar model name substitute for evidence

Quantities, units and bookkeeping: Identify length, area, volume, time and mass behind a unit label; Convert millimeters to meters and hours to seconds before combining values; Explain that water depth over a known area corresponds to a volume; Distinguish meters per hour from meters received during a timestep; Convert volume per time to an area-normalized flow, and back, using the actual catchment area; Recognize when water density is needed and when a variable's name is misleading; Distinguish square meters from a fraction of a larger catchment; Check that both sides of an equation represent the same kind of quantity; Explain why dividing comparable quantities removes their units; State whether a positive value means adding water, losing water or increasing dryness; Explain why more stored water can mean a smaller deficit, and why those updates have opposite signs; Calculate what remains after accounting for starting water, inflows, outflows and final water; Use area fractions rather than treating unequal parts of a catchment equally; Distinguish meaningful measurement detail from digits printed by a computer

Algebra, functions, slopes and distributions: Read subscripts as labels, superscripts as powers, bars as averages and Greek letters as named quantities; Solve for a starting state or parameter without changing the relationship; Treat a formula as a mapping and understand when its result can be mapped back uniquely; Distinguish proportional changes from responses that change strength with the current state; Understand repeated multiplication and how an exponential responds to positive and negative arguments; Understand ln as the inverse of exp, including why its input must be positive; Unpack products, quotients and exponentials when following a TOPMODEL derivation; Recognize that changing the numeric unit convention can shift a logged index or parameter; never swap conventions silently; Relate elevation change divided by horizontal distance to tan of the slope angle; Distinguish a straight line in ordinary coordinates from one on a log plot; Understand bins, bin edges, representative values and the amount of area assigned to each bin; Distinguish the fraction below a threshold from the fraction above it; Estimate between known endpoints and recognize when extrapolation goes beyond available information; Translate a sum into an accumulation loop, with its index range and weights intact; Explain when a physical state changes which branch of a formula applies

Calculus, introduced from quantities the learner can picture: Calculate the difference between two amounts and the elapsed time; Interpret a graph's rise divided by its run; Ask how fast something is changing near one moment rather than over a whole storm; Understand the idea of looking at progressively smaller intervals; Interpret the local slope of a function; recognize dS/dt as a storage-change rate; Explain why differentiating storage with respect to time produces a flow-like quantity; Add small contributions over time or over pieces of area; Interpret an accumulated total with a start and end, rather than treating the integral sign as decorative notation; Distinguish time integration from area or depth integration; Link a changing stored amount to the flow that builds or drains it; Follow constant, linear, power, exponential and logarithmic terms that occur in the relevant derivations; Track how changing storage changes an exponential discharge function through its argument; Understand a rule for how state changes, with an initial value needed to obtain a trajectory; Follow simple storage–outflow derivations and explain how starting conditions fix the otherwise unknown constant; Recognize dependence on several variables and spatial change; full multivariable calculus is not needed to run this implementation; Connect rectangular/trapezoidal area estimates to numerical sums used by the program

Numerical methods and floating-point behavior: Replace continuous time or space with finite steps or classes; Calculate using known earlier state, then commit the new state; Understand that rain, drainage, evaporation and runoff branches may give different results if reordered; Distinguish error caused by finite steps from error caused by floating-point rounding; Distinguish a physically changing result from numerical growth caused by the calculation scheme; Check whether results settle as timestep or class resolution is refined; Ask whether the numerical rule approaches the intended equation as the step shrinks; Narrow an interval around a solution by repeatedly dividing it; Use a function and its slope to improve an estimated solution; Distinguish a small update from a sufficiently solved equation; Identify what happens when a solver fails to finish, including whole-process termination; Inspect division by zero, log of zero, and subtracting almost equal exponentials; Distinguish meaningful physical bounds from small-value cleanup that changes accounting; Select absolute, relative or exact comparisons according to the test's purpose; Explain why a finite-looking final hydrograph cannot replace checks inside the computation; Preserve arithmetic order and precision when assessing a language translation

Water in air, plants and soil: Distinguish the weather input from water already in the catchment; Understand water held by vegetation or surface features before it reaches soil; Distinguish water leaving exposed surfaces from water released through plants; Separate atmospheric demand from what the available soil water can supply; Picture the spaces that can hold air or water; Distinguish the amount of water in soil from the fraction of pore space filled; Understand the state in which the relevant pore space is filled with water; Locate partly water-filled and water-filled soil regions; Distinguish its depth below the ground from a storage deficit expressed as water depth; Understand the root-zone reference condition used for deficit accounting; do not equate it with full saturation; Understand the part of soil from which plants obtain water; Distinguish entry through the soil surface from later movement within soil; Distinguish downward movement from water delivered to the saturated store; Understand how readily water moves through a soil under specified conditions; Distinguish the driving force for water movement from the amount of stored water; Connect flow to conductivity, cross section and head gradient before using a hillslope approximation; Distinguish a layer's combined ability to carry flow from conductivity at one depth; Understand why relatively dry soil can draw water toward a wetting front; Recognize when a single averaged soil description misses contrasting layers, cracks or large pores

Catchments and runoff pathways: Identify the land area contributing water to a chosen outlet; Identify the boundary between neighboring drainage areas; Distinguish the parts used to describe where water reaches channels; Trace connected flow paths to the outlet; Picture flow gathering into hollows or spreading across ridges; Distinguish water moving over the ground from water moving through it; Understand surface runoff caused by rainfall arriving faster than soil can accept it; Understand surface runoff caused by a lack of remaining storage; Understand subsurface water reaching the surface again; Distinguish slower drainage from rapid changes during a storm without assuming each is a perfectly separable water source; Understand why the part producing rapid runoff expands and contracts as the catchment wets and dries; Distinguish a saturated patch from one that can actually deliver water to the stream; Explain why identical rainfall can produce different runoff after a wet week and a dry week; Read rising flow, peak, lag, falling limb and accumulated discharge

Spatial simplification and the topographic index: Distinguish one catchment average from tracking every location separately; Group locations expected to respond alike rather than preserving every pixel as a model state; Identify how much land drains toward a location; Divide contributing area by contour width; do not substitute total area without that normalization; Interpret ln(a/tan beta) and explain the role of both contributing area and slope; Understand the catchment reference value used to compare one class with the average; Explain what a histogram preserves and what location/connectivity detail it loses; Preserve the high-to-low convention assumed in runoff integration; Distinguish an index value from the area distribution paired with it; Explain why code accesses the next area entry and why allocation exceeds the main class count; Connect adjacent class values and weights to the program's trapezoidal-style calculations; Distinguish a terrain-based wetness tendency from a measured moisture map

TOPMODEL assumptions and the deficit–flow relationships: Distinguish the assumption used to infer a spatial pattern from the time-varying catchment run; Identify where one recharge description substitutes for varying local conditions; Explain the physical shortcut and when it might fail; Understand the assumed connection between increasing deficit and declining lateral drainage; Connect a catchment-average dryness state to each index class; Explain every term in `deficit_local = sbar + szm*(tl-lnaotb)` and its sign; Distinguish `szm` from a direct soil depth and explain its sensitivity role; Explain `qb = szq*exp(-sbar/szm)` and the direction of its response; Trace how `szq` is calculated rather than treating it as an unrelated fitted constant; Distinguish the numeric value read as `t0` from the physical quantity obtained through exponentiation; Invert the exponential relationship and state its positive-input requirements; Connect local deficit, unsaturated storage and excess water; avoid assuming the mean deficit alone is the local condition; Explain why recharge reduces `sbar` and baseflow increases it; Identify which assumptions support the outlet flow prediction and which support the spatial saturation prediction

Root-zone and unsaturated-zone timestep mechanics: Follow rainfall reducing the amount of water needed to reach the reference condition; Follow water left after the root-zone deficit has been filled; Distinguish water waiting to drain from root-zone deficit and saturated-zone deficit; Follow excess when unsaturated water exceeds the allowed local deficit; Interpret the `td`, deficit and timestep factors in the drainage expression through a unit audit; Explain why calculated drainage cannot exceed available unsaturated water; Trace the root-zone deficit's effect on actual evaporation; Prevent removing more water than the root-zone representation permits; Distinguish local class amounts from whole-catchment totals; Understand interpolation at a threshold between classes; Distinguish state needed for the next step from values recomputed for output; Understand why a balance check must account for initial deficits and stores

Optional infiltration-excess calculations: Picture a simplified boundary between wetter and drier soil; Explain `hf`, `dth` and their product physically; Distinguish the implemented extension from a constant-conductivity infiltration approximation; Track the conversion from amount per timestep into intensity used by the infiltration solver; Identify when water begins accumulating at the surface because intake cannot keep up; Distinguish a storm starting unponded from one already ponded; Distinguish `cumf` from the increment `df` returned for one step; Identify which variables must persist between wet steps and when dry conditions reset them; Follow the bracket search and later iterative solution, including small-value branches; Understand what is implied when infiltration excess is applied over the modeled area; Recognize that tests with `infex=0` cannot establish correctness of the infiltration branch

Routing: when generated runoff reaches the outlet: Separate creating local runoff from delaying its arrival downstream; Calculate time from distance and velocity with matching units; Distinguish `chv` and `rv` and the paths each represents; Describe how contributing area is distributed with distance along drainage paths; Convert distance/area information into fractions arriving at later times; Understand the individual weights in the response array; Explain output as the sum of delayed contributions from several earlier inputs; Understand when separate runoff pulses can be added without changing the routing weights; Recognize the paper's flow-dependent routing as a separate concept from the later constant-velocity implementation; Distinguish movement of water from movement of a flow disturbance; introduce this before evaluating routing assumptions; Trace `num_delay`, histogram length and scheduled future values in `Q`; Check weight sums and account for water still queued at the end of a run; Understand initial baseflow in the queue and the recession remaining after forcing ends; Avoid routing the same flow twice when coupling the model to a larger system

Terrain and parameter preparation: Understand a raster of terrain heights and what its pixel size means; Distinguish grid cells from catchment polygons and channel lines; Separate geographic coordinates from projected distances suitable for area and slope calculations; Prevent computing slopes or distances from incompatible coordinate scales; Distinguish missing terrain from zero elevation and excluded cells; Understand why an elevation raster may not yield continuous drainage paths directly; Follow how upslope contributing area is computed from terrain; Recognize that different flow-direction rules can give different index distributions; Verify that the selected outlet and polygon refer to the same drainage area; Handle zero or near-zero slope before dividing or taking a logarithm; Preserve compatible cell locations when combining layers; Turn raster values within one catchment into an area-weighted distribution; Understand class edges, counts, weights and resolution effects before producing `subcat.dat`; Distinguish an input distance raster from the final routing histogram; Understand height above drainage, watershed identifiers and the connected catchment dataset used by the workflow; Separate terrain preprocessing tools from the runtime hydrological model; Retain data versions, projection, resolution, tool settings and commands with generated parameters; Verify representative shapes and invariants without reading every large raster or GeoJSON into an agent context

Observations, calibration and scientific testing: Distinguish having measured flow for evaluation from having to predict without it; Understand why a point gauge may not represent rainfall over the whole area; Understand measurement uncertainty and conversion from a measured water level to estimated flow where applicable; Match observations and simulations by interval, timestamp convention and units; Distinguish selecting parameters using data from testing predictions on independent data; Distinguish a local physical measurement from a value compensating for unresolved spatial variation; Vary an input or parameter deliberately and examine what output changes; Understand why the effect of one parameter can depend on another; Distinguish individual errors, persistent direction of error and penalties favoring large errors; Understand the score optimized during fitting and what it neglects; Evaluate these separately rather than letting one score hide a failure; Interpret a score relative to its comparison model; check the exact formula in `results` before naming it; Use falling flows to reason about storage and drainage parameters; Ask whether available observations can actually distinguish two parameter choices; Recognize that different parameter combinations can produce similarly good outputs; Separate tuning data from wet, dry, seasonal and independent-event evaluation; Distinguish model adjustment from the period intended for evaluation; Test saturation patterns, soil wetness or other internal predictions instead of evaluating outlet discharge alone; Separate forcing, observations, parameters, initial state, numerical approximation and model structure; Propose a test that could disprove an explanation, not merely another parameter setting that improves a score

Validity limits and alternative explanations: Compare the assumptions against the actual catchment rather than using model popularity as evidence; Ask whether modeled stores and assumed subsurface patterns remain plausible; Examine water that does not follow the shallow surface drainage pattern; Ask which surface controls subsurface flow; Question a local surface slope used as the driving gradient; Test whether a single relation can represent distinct flow pathways; Determine whether pipes and paved surfaces need separate representations; Distinguish missing processes from bad rainfall-runoff parameter choices; Identify assumptions hidden by basin-wide forcing or demand; Ask whether parameters and index distributions remain meaningful at a different grid size or catchment scale; Distinguish adjustable rates from a missing process or wrong connectivity; Compare a simple bucket, spatial infiltration model, explicit hillslope model and dynamic TOPMODEL at the level needed to choose further investigation

Legacy Fortran literacy: Identify comment lines, label columns, continuation markers and statement text; Understand why text past a column limit may not be compiled as expected; Separate capitalization used for readability from distinct identifiers; Recover types from declarations and the default naming rules; recognize that a misspelling can create a new variable; Distinguish numeric categories and precision, including mixed expressions; Recognize decimal/exponent forms and calls such as EXP, ALOG and ABS; Distinguish updating a variable from `.EQ.` comparisons; Read `.LT.`, `.LE.`, `.GT.`, `.GE.`, `.NE.`, `.AND.`, `.OR.` and `.NOT.` correctly; Distinguish procedure roles and where results or side effects appear; Determine which caller values a subroutine can modify; do not assume C value-copy behavior; Identify shared storage and verify matching field order, type and shape in every declaring routine; Determine the actual lifetime of values; do not assume every local variable safely remembers the previous call; Distinguish initialization from a per-call assignment and learn how persistence must be established; Read one-based arrays and any explicitly different bounds; Understand the first index's storage stride for multidimensional arrays when translating layouts; Preserve the final iteration and any non-unit loop increment; Reconstruct branch and loop control before replacing it with structured C++; Distinguish a labeled no-op from C/C++ continue semantics; Understand fixed-length strings, padding and file-name limits; Connect OPEN, READ, WRITE and CLOSE to file handles or streams; Decode record layouts and numeric/string formatting; Recognize repeated array reads or writes inside one statement; Distinguish terminating the whole process from returning to the caller; Distinguish standard language behavior from behavior tolerated by an older compiler

Translating Fortran behavior into C++: Preserve behavior and state transitions before changing architecture or notation; Map COMMON blocks to an explicit model-state object rather than unrelated globals; Preserve modifications made through Fortran arguments; Label each argument as read, written, or both; do not infer that role from its name; Choose deliberate one-based compatibility or a fully reviewed zero-based conversion; Preserve access to boundary/sentinel cells when converting array sizes; Preserve inclusive bounds, iteration order and jumps out of nested loops; Distinguish reproducing the old calculation from intentionally improving precision; Detect where a real-valued Fortran quantity becomes an integer in the C interface; Prevent moving a value that survives a storm loop into a temporary local recreated every update; Ensure every read has a defined prior write or documented initialized source; Understand how shared arguments and arrays constrain safe reordering; Replace process exits with explicit failures only while preserving a defined model state; Compare old/new intermediate states and branch decisions, not only the final outlet result; Document them separately so a changed hydrograph has an identifiable cause; Learn modules, derived types, intent, allocatable arrays and ISO_C_BINDING when modernizing; they are not prerequisites for reading this legacy file

Repository architecture and execution ownership: Separate hydrological calculations from how a host controls and queries them; Distinguish the demonstration executable from an external simulation orchestrator; Identify the structure owning stores, arrays, counters, parameters and file handles; Distinguish creating the function table/state container from reading configuration and establishing valid state; Trace one model advance and later resource cleanup; Locate the loop in the original program and explain its move to the host in the BMI adaptation; Distinguish the historical multi-subcatchment program from one framework-managed instance; Identify who supplies forcing and who owns the output schedule in each mode; Trace `topmod.run` to forcing, terrain, parameter and output paths; Recognize positional files where reordered fields silently change meaning or fail parsing; Identify what must be recomputed when calibration changes a parameter; Trace allocations, borrowed pointers, reallocations and corresponding frees; Test whether two model instances can run without sharing mutable simulation state; Verify current source when older instructions name removed build paths or describe outdated behavior

BMI contracts, units and clocks: Connect the C callbacks to the behavior a C++ interface would promise; Distinguish advertised input, output and parameter names from internal state names; Verify what a long exchange name means by inspecting its pointer mapping and units; Ensure a caller allocates and interprets the right memory; Distinguish a value snapshot from a borrowed view whose lifetime matters; Verify index conventions, bounds, element size and error handling; Understand why a catchment-scale exchange can advertise a scalar grid despite internal class arrays; Distinguish a deliberate BMI failure response from uninitialized metadata; Separate model time from array indices and elapsed-step counts; Verify behavior for exact, fractional, repeated, backward and beyond-end requests; Make sure rate/depth conventions and timestamps agree across coupled components; Distinguish changing a scalar from updating all derived states and routing arrays dependent on it; Understand extern C, exception containment and allocation ownership across languages; Distinguish returning success from actually satisfying the caller's requested operation

Checkpoints, serialization and restart: Identify every value needed to continue a run, including delayed runoff still in the queue; Distinguish values that must be restored from those supplied by the destination model's configuration; Distinguish continuing the original clock from importing a hydrological state into a new run; Follow the reserved BMI controls and data/length exchange in their required order; Identify who allocates, copies, retains and releases serialized bytes; Understand why reading the same values in a different order is not a compatible format; Detect payloads created under incompatible field layouts; Validate counts before allocation and preserve one-based endpoint storage; Distinguish same-build restart from an archive promised to work across architectures or library versions; Test whether failed loading leaves the instance safe and whether rollback is required; Recognize the serialization implementation's explicit rejection of standalone mode; Compare all relevant outputs after uninterrupted and interrupted runs, including several restart points; Recognize that omitted solver memory or routing history can produce divergence later rather than immediately; Understand the vector-backed buffer sufficiently to investigate truncated archives, capacity changes or EOF handling

Build, packaging and operational behavior: Identify C science/BMI files and C++ serialization files in each build target; Understand why adding one C++ source affects linking and sanitizer runtime requirements; Distinguish a loadable component from a standalone executable; Diagnose Boost serialization discovery separately from application source compilation; Understand what each catches and what hydrological errors neither can detect; Distinguish compile-time logging settings from model output-file switches; Identify relative paths that make a binary work only from a particular directory; Inspect what is distributed versus what was available only in the source checkout; Separate runner/toolchain/dependency failures from model failures; Reason about compute and memory cost from loop and allocation sizes; Do not infer an MPI hydrological solver merely because terrain preparation uses MPI tools; Inspect file I/O, repeated allocation, buffers and cleanup across many instances or calibration runs

Testing the software and the science separately: Distinguish implementing the chosen equations correctly from representing real catchment behavior adequately; Locate the boundary and failure being isolated; Explain why the expected answer is trustworthy; Preserve prior behavior while recognizing that an old baseline can contain an old defect; Use identical configurations, forcing, precision assumptions and intermediate comparisons; Use tiny stores, simple arithmetic and short routing queues to make errors visible; Account for all stores, deficits, fluxes and pending routed water; Test storage, deficit, evaporation and area-fraction constraints; Inspect drainage and evaporation without new precipitation; Exercise threshold transitions rather than only middle-of-range conditions; Test ponding, no ponding, cessation and storm restart with the branch enabled; Check exact queue positions, weight sums and tail drainage; Test non-unit and fractional steps to expose hidden hourly assumptions; Predict relationships between carefully controlled runs when a full exact answer is unavailable; Test missing files, short records, invalid counts, unsafe dimensions and invalid physical values; Test advertised counts, names, types, units, bounds and derived recomputation; Interleave two runs and compare them with separately executed references; Test the distinct clock semantics as well as hydrological state restoration; Justify exact equality for same-build restart where expected, and suitable numeric tolerances for cross-implementation comparisons; Understand why clean memory diagnostics do not establish correct equations, units or physical assumptions; Use held-out storms, seasons and catchments where appropriate; Record commit, build, inputs, branch settings, first divergent state and the smallest reproducing case

Paper-specific reading tasks: Identify what the authors wanted to simplify without discarding spatial effects; Connect runoff mechanisms to the proposed storage/area relationship; Identify interception, infiltration and subsurface storage roles without replacing them with the later code's terminology; Trace assumptions, local flow, storage distribution and contributing area, checking notation and signs; Follow headwater/sideslope contributions and the original nonlinear travel rule; Distinguish field measurements, estimates and optimization; Identify the tested catchments, conditions and observations; Read the compared error measures and parameter response surfaces; Distinguish successful tested behavior from components insufficiently exercised by the data; Map paper claims to later Fortran and current code explicitly; annotate changed or absent components

Concrete review cases found in the current source: Infiltration intensity narrowing: `topmod` calculates a double `rint`, but `expinf` takes `int rint` (U04, P09, I04. Test a fractional positive intensity and compare the passed value with the intended rate.)[cite: 1]; Uninitialized infiltration quantity: `expinf` declares local `dth` and uses it in `cd=hf*dth` without assigning it in that function; the caller does not pass it (F11, P11, I02. Trace the Fortran COMMON source, then test the enabled branch with defined soil inputs.)[cite: 1]; Storm memory: `topmod` initializes `irof` and `cumf` on each call; `irof` is passed by value (P03, P10, I08. Compare a continuous storm across multiple update calls with the legacy loop's state evolution.)[cite: 1]; Fractional-time handling: Update increments a step field by dt; Update_until calls an additional Update after assigning the fractional dt, even if the fraction is zero (B09–B10, Q13. Probe exact-step, fractional-step and repeated-time requests and inspect state mutation.)[cite: 1]; Future routing contributions: The routing loop breaks when its destination index exceeds current_time_step (R07, R11–R13, Q12. Inspect queue contents after a pulse; compare expected future deposits in standalone and coupled modes.)[cite: 1]; Logged parameter ambiguity: Documentation describes physical transmissivity while initialization uses `t0` inside an exponential and adds log(dt) (M06–M08, A09–A10. Trace file value through initialization and audit units before calibration.)[cite: 1]; Misleading comment: A comment calls `tl` related to time lag, while the terrain reader derives it from index values and weights (T06, E14. Follow assignments rather than expanding the acronym from the comment.)[cite: 1]; Baseline-test scope: Test documentation describes historical exact-output comparisons, while current CMake/CI define separate BMI, serialization and restart targets (Q03–Q05, O09. Identify what each current test actually asserts; do not treat old prose as a current test result.)[cite: 1]

Essential symbol crosswalk: SBAR: sbar (Catchment mean saturation deficit; larger is drier)[cite: 1]; SD: deficit_local (Saturation deficit assigned to an index class)[cite: 1]; SRZ: deficit_root_zone (Root-zone deficit relative to its reference condition)[cite: 1]; SUZ: stor_unsat_zone (Water stored in the unsaturated-zone representation)[cite: 1]; SZM: szm (Exponential deficit scale)[cite: 1]; T0: t0 (Logged transmissivity-related input; inspect transformations)[cite: 1]; SZQ: szq (Derived baseflow scale)[cite: 1]; TL: tl (Mean topographic-index quantity)[cite: 1]; ST: lnaotb (Topographic-index values)[cite: 1]; AC: dist_area_lnaotb (Area distribution associated with index intervals)[cite: 1]; TD: td (Unsaturated drainage-delay parameter; audit dimensional convention)[cite: 1]; SRMAX: srmax (Maximum root-zone deficit)[cite: 1]; SR0: sr0 (Initial root-zone deficit)[cite: 1]; Q0: Q0 (Initial flow used to establish the starting state)[cite: 1]; R, PE: rain, pe (Supplied rain and potential-evaporation series)[cite: 1]; P, EP: p, ep (Current-step working rain and evaporation-demand quantities)[cite: 1]; QUZ: quz (Area-weighted recharge quantity computed in the class loop)[cite: 1]; QB: qb (Saturated-zone drainage/baseflow quantity)[cite: 1]; QOF: qof (Generated overland-flow quantity)[cite: 1]; Q: Q (Routed output/history queue, depending on execution mode)[cite: 1]; CA: contrib_area (Contributing-area diagnostic)[cite: 1]; CHV, RV: chv, rv (Channel and internal routing velocities)[cite: 1]; AR: time_delay_histogram (Delayed-arrival weights)[cite: 1]; ACH: cum_dist_area_with_dist (Cumulative contributing area with distance)[cite: 1]; D: dist_from_outlet (Distances used to construct travel times)[cite: 1]; ND, NR: num_delay, num_time_delay_histo_ords (Initial delay and routing-histogram length)[cite: 1]; INFEX: infex (Optional infiltration-excess branch switch)[cite: 1]; XK0, HF, DTH: xk0, hf, dth (Conductivity, wetting-front suction and water-content change)[cite: 1]; IROF, CUMF, DF: irof, cumf, df (Ponding flag, cumulative infiltration and incremental infiltration)[cite: 1]; BAL: bal (Water-balance accounting quantity)[cite: 1]

Teaching order and completion standard: Explain the model's water pathways and assumptions in ordinary language; Derive and hand-calculate a small deficit/baseflow example with correct units; Trace a complete timestep through root-zone, unsaturated, saturated and routing state; Read the historical Fortran and explain an equivalent C++ control/data flow; Distinguish paper behavior, later model changes and current interface behavior; Explain every model exchange, its units, lifetime and clock convention; Design tests that distinguish a porting bug, a unit error, a restart omission and an invalid physical assumption; Make a bounded change with an explicit impact analysis and meaningful verification
